title: Agastya's gifts
hook: the sage who digested a demon hands Rama a bow made by Vishvakarma, and Hindus still bless their tools at Ayudha Puja
carry: ayudha puja: what you hold is blessed for dharma

segments.voice: Yesterday: ahimsa, and a bow carried only to protect. Sita asked whether carrying weapons would change Rama, and he answered with his promise.

On the way to Agastya, Rama tells Lakshmana a story about him, the kind people tell about a legend before you meet one. Two demon brothers, Ilvala and Vatapi, used to trap holy men. Ilvala would turn Vatapi into a ram, cook him, and serve him to a guest. Then he'd call his brother's name, and Vatapi would burst out of the guest's body, killing him. It worked many times. Until they served the meal to Agastya.
screen: `ILVALA AND VATAPI.` → `A RAM SERVED TO GUESTS.` → `UNTIL THEY FED AGASTYA.`

segments.voice: Agastya ate the meal. Ilvala called: Vatapi, come out. Nothing happened. Agastya had simply digested him, and when Ilvala attacked in fury, the sage burned him with a look. Many families still say a short prayer naming Agastya after a big meal, asking to digest it as he did. Since then, Rama says, the south has been safe for sages. The old sage welcomes them with water and food, and then, unasked, gives Rama weapons. A great bow adorned with gold, made by Vishvakarma, the craftsman of the gods, once Vishnu's. An arrow from Brahma that never misses. Two quivers from Indra that never run out. And a sword in a golden sheath. Remember Sita's worry: what weapons do to the one who carries them. Look at how these come: from a man of tapas, freely, with a blessing, for protecting others. Hindus still mark this idea every year. At Navaratri, on Ayudha Puja, many families, especially in the south, lay their tools before the Goddess: books, instruments, a laptop, the car. In parts of the east, Vishvakarma himself gets a puja in workshops and factories. The thought behind both: what you hold is a gift, to be used for dharma, never against it. Then Agastya gives one more gift, advice. Near the Godavari is a lovely place called Panchavati. Live there, and protect the sages from there.
screen: `AGASTYA DIGESTS A DEMON.` · `A BOW MADE BY VISHVAKARMA.` · `GIVEN FREELY, FOR PROTECTION.` · `AYUDHA PUJA: TOOLS BLESSED.` · then, large: `GO TO PANCHAVATI.`

segments.voice: In many Hindu homes, if your foot touches a book, you touch it and bring your hand to your forehead: the tools of learning are sacred. Pick up something you work with, a pen, your phone, a tool, and hold it in both hands. If you pray, offer it the way families do at Ayudha Puja, and ask that it be used for good. If you don't, name one good thing it will do this week, and breathe.
Agastya's weapons. Vishnu's bow, Brahma's arrow, Indra's two quivers and a golden sword, given by the sage for protecting others.
Your line: ayudha puja: what you hold is blessed for dharma. Next stop, a place by the river called Panchavati. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Agastya is honored in tradition as the great sage of the south, and the story of Vatapi and Ilvala is a familiar one in Hindu storytelling. Ayudha Puja, near the end of Navaratri, is widely kept in South India, and Vishvakarma Puja in parts of eastern India.
